commit.message:
Implement replica recovery

A replica that crashed and lost its memory can now rejoin safely. This
is the recovery protocol of section 4.3 of the paper, with the fix that
Michael et al. showed it needs.

Replica::recover builds a replica in recovering status. It sends
Recovery, with a nonce, to every other replica, re-sends it on idle,
and until it has recovered it acts on nothing else: not Prepare, not a
view change, not a client request. Replicas in normal status answer
RecoveryResponse with their view; the primary of that view includes its
log and commit number. With a quorum of responses carrying its nonce,
including one from the primary of the latest view among them, the
recovering replica installs that primary's log, executes the committed
prefix, and returns to normal in that view.

One thing has to survive the crash: the view number. The library asks
its owner to persist Replica::view_number after every step, before
delivering what the step produced, and to pass it to recover. A
recovering replica will not rejoin a view older than the one it
persisted. Without that, as Michael et al. show, a replica can send
StartViewChange, crash, recover in the old view because nobody has
moved yet, and then its old message completes a view change it no
longer knows it started, so two views run at once. The persisted view
also travels in Recovery: a replica behind it takes that as the request
for the view change the crashed replica had started and forgotten, and
starts it, which is what the lost StartViewChange would have done.
Otherwise a replica that persisted a view nobody else ever entered
would wait forever.

The state transfer status is renamed StateTransfer so it is not
confused with recovering.

The simulator persists each replica's view before its messages go out
and rebuilds a rebooted replica with Replica::recover, drawing the
nonce from the seed. It limits reboots to fewer than f replicas
recovering at once, since a replica without its memory counts as
failed until recovered, and the liveness core is drawn so that it holds
a quorum of replicas that are not recovering, for the same reason.
Durability now counts holders among the replicas that are not
recovering, against the quorums those replicas could form. The kvstore
example keeps the view number in a file next to the binary and comes
back through recovery when the file exists.

Add a cluster test where a replica reboots, ignores an op that arrives
while it is recovering, recovers from the others' responses with the
primary's log, and takes part in the next op.

Found by the simulator at commit 949b3d7, where a rebooted replica
simply rejoined and 382 of 5695 seeds failed, for example

    cargo run --release -p vsr-simulator -- --lite 10677592078291100242

whose log installation assertion fired at tick 43726 after a view
change had lost a committed op. With this change 7051 random seeds pass
with no failure, including that one, the durability failure of seed
10267825576565313013, and the split brain of seed 10080230919357778125.

Simulate real crashes: a restarted replica may come back with no memory

Until now a crashed replica kept its state and a restart resumed it, as
if it had only been paused. That is not what a crash does to a replica
that keeps everything in memory. A restart now has a per-seed
probability of being a reboot: the replica is replaced by a fresh one
with an empty log, view 0, and no memory of what it acknowledged or
which views it took part in. The properties that track state per
replica start over for a rebooted one.

This is the failing test for the recovery protocol of section 4.3 of
the paper, which the library does not implement: a rebooted replica
rejoins as a normal backup, or worse, as the primary of view 0. In a
30 second batch, 382 of 5695 seeds failed, in three ways:

- A replica that had committed ops received a log without them. The
  library's own assertion that an installed log holds the committed
  prefix fires, for example with

      cargo run --release -p vsr-simulator -- --lite 10677592078291100242

  at tick 43726. That is committed data lost in a view change after
  a replica that had acknowledged it forgot.

- Durability: a replica committed an op that fewer than a quorum of
  replicas hold, for example

      cargo run --release -p vsr-simulator -- 10267825576565313013

  at tick 190613 with 2 of 4 replicas holding the op.

- Two replicas committed different ops at the same index. A rebooted
  replica 0 believes it is the primary of view 0 in normal status,
  accepts re-sent client requests, and another rebooted replica
  acknowledges them, so view 0 commits a second history next to the
  live view's. That is the split brain the paper's section 8 warns of,
  and what recovery's "recovering" status prevents.

Also fix the replies property, which sliced the log of the replica that
had committed furthest even after that replica rebooted and its log
had shrunk.

Rename the README's ToDo list to Protocol support

It lists what the protocol implementation covers, not chores. The
simulator is not a protocol feature and has its own section, and the
client table and retransmission were missing from the list.

Credit TigerBeetle in the README and include its license

The stepped replica and the simulator's design follow TigerBeetle, so
say so in the references and carry its Apache 2.0 license text.

Step the replica and client instead of handing them channels

The library did no I/O, but it still owned two channel senders that
every handler pushed into: one for messages to other replicas, one for
replies to clients. That made crossbeam-channel a dependency, put its
Sender type in the public API, and forced the replica's state behind
Cell, RefCell, and atomics so handlers could take &self. It also hid
what a step produced.

Follow TigerBeetle's shape, and Betelgeuse's: a Replica and a Client
are state machines their owner steps. on_message, on_reply, and on_idle
take &mut self; what they want sent accumulates in an outbox that the
owner drains afterwards with drain_messages, drain_replies, and drain,
and delivers however it likes: over sockets, through a simulated
network, or straight into another replica in a test. The replica owns
its state machine, whose apply now takes &mut self, and exposes it for
inspection. Config is a plain value each replica and client holds a
copy of. The client callback is gone; on_reply returns whether the
reply answered the pending request. The library depends on log alone.

The simulator hands outboxes to its network after every step, delivers
replies to the clients directly, and drops its channel dependency too.
Its network gained a send method in place of draining a receiver. The
cluster tests gained a small Cluster helper that queues what replicas
and the client produce and delivers it under the test's control, which
replaces the setup every test repeated. The kvstore example keeps its
threads for sockets and timers, using std::sync::mpsc to feed the one
thread that owns the replica, and flushes the outboxes after every
event.

Protocol code is unchanged apart from the mechanics; all seeds tried
pass as before and clippy is clean across the workspace, since the Arc
around Config that it kept flagging is gone.

Drop parking_lot and make env_logger a dev-dependency

Neither is used by the library. parking_lot only backed the mutex in the
test accumulator, which std::sync::Mutex does just as well, and
env_logger is only initialized by tests and examples.

Back off the view change timeout after each failed view change

A replica waited the same primary timeout for every view change. When
that timeout is shorter than a view change takes, which happens with
short heartbeat intervals and delayed or lost messages, some replica's
timer fires before the change completes, starts the next view, and
every other replica adopts it and restarts its own timer. Nothing ever
completes and the cluster is livelocked.

Each view change entered while already in a view change, whether on the
replica's own timer or by adopting a view another replica started, now
doubles the wait before the next one, capped at 2^10 times the base
timeout. Returning to normal status resets it. The wait soon exceeds
the time a view change takes, one completes, and normal operation
resumes. The paper only says that liveness depends on setting timeouts
properly; this is how TigerBeetle sets them.

Add a cluster test that cuts a backup off and checks that the idle
periods between the view changes it starts are one, two, and four
timeouts.

Found by the simulator at commit 06ba5de with

    SEED=12458081382810450947 cargo run --release -p vsr-simulator

which stalled at 1739 of 10000 requests for a million ticks: a
heartbeat every tick, a five tick timeout, six replicas, and after a
crash the views advanced forever. With this change the seed passes in
61342 ticks.

Add the kvstore example: a multi-node key-value store over TCP

Every node runs one replica in a thread that owns it; other threads turn
peer connections, client connections, and a 100 ms tick into events for
that thread. Nodes exchange protocol messages as one line of text each,
connecting to each other on demand and dropping connections on error,
since the protocol re-sends what matters. Every node accepts client
connections speaking a Redis-like inline protocol with SET, GET, and
PING, so nc works as a client. A node that is not the primary forwards
the request through its own vsr_rs::Client and routes the reply back to
the connection, so any node can be talked to. GET goes through the log
too, so it is linearizable.

Client ids encode the node that owns the connection, so the primary
knows where to send the reply, and the node's start time, so a restarted
node never reuses an id. Without that, the primary's client table took a
new connection's first request for a re-send of an old one with the same
id and answered it from its cache, returning a stale value: the client
recovery problem of section 4.5 of the paper.

The README walks through starting three nodes, talking to them, killing
the primary and watching the view change, and restarting the node. It
also spells out the limitations, in particular that a restarted node
comes back empty and catches up from the primary, which is not the
paper's recovery protocol.

Standard library only for networking and threads, plus the crossbeam
channel the library already uses for messages.

Implement view changes

When the primary fails, the backups must agree on a new one and on the
log it starts from, without losing anything a client was told had
committed. This is the view change protocol of section 4.2 of the paper.

A backup that has not heard from the primary for Config::primary_timeout
idle periods moves to the next view, sets its status to view-change, and
sends StartViewChange to every replica. A replica that hears of a higher
view this way adopts it rather than counting up on its own, as the TLA+
analysis recommends. With StartViewChange from f other replicas, a
replica sends DoViewChange to the new view's primary, carrying its log,
its commit number, and the last view in which it was normal. With a
quorum of those, the new primary takes the log from the latest normal
view, the longest if several, which by quorum intersection holds every
committed op, commits what the votes say is committed, replies to the
clients for anything the old primary did not get to, and sends
StartView. Backups replace their log with it, commit up to the commit
number in it, and acknowledge the rest, which the new primary then
commits as usual. Idle periods re-send StartViewChange and DoViewChange,
and a view change that itself takes primary_timeout idle periods is
followed by one for the next view, in case the new primary is down too.

A replica that receives Prepare or Commit from a later view, or from
its own view while it is still changing to it, has missed the change.
It asks the new primary for the log from its commit number on, and only
when the reply arrives replaces the suffix of its log with it. This is
the state transfer fix from the TLA+ analysis: the paper truncates to
the commit number first, which can drop a committed op below a majority
if the reply never comes. Within a view, state transfer still merges
by op number as before. A StartView for a view the replica is already
normal in is ignored, so a replayed one cannot replace a newer log.
The commit number never moves backwards, and a log is only installed if
it contains the replica's committed prefix; the client table is rebuilt
from the new log, keeping the replies of committed requests.

Replies carry the view number and the client adopts it, so its next
request goes to the new primary. Every reply also lets the client
discard duplicates, and the client already re-sends to all replicas on
idle, which is how a request outlives a primary.

The simulator draws the primary timeout from the seed, bounded below by
a few times the mean network delay so that most delayed heartbeats do
not look like a dead primary, and its properties no longer assume that
replica 0 is the primary: durability is checked on whichever replica
commits, expected replies come from whichever replica has committed
furthest, and duplicate ops are checked in the committed prefix only,
since a view change may replace entries beyond it. Its own tests now
run with crashes and a random core.

Add a cluster test where the primary crashes with an op prepared on the
backups but uncommitted: the backups change view, the new primary
commits the op and replies, and the client follows it to the new view.

The failing simulator run was

    SEED=5 cargo run --release -p vsr-simulator -- --lite

at commit 5f4c413, whose core excluded the primary and which stopped
with "no state convergence: pending commit". Every seed tried passes
now, including cores without replica 0 and full runs with hundreds of
crashes and restarts, and a batch of 5815 random seeds found no
failure. One seed, 12458081382810450947, livelocks: with a heartbeat
every tick and a five tick timeout, view changes keep starting before
the previous one can complete. That needs backoff on the view change
timeout and is left for the next change.

Crash and restart replicas in the simulator, with a liveness core

Replicas can now crash: a crashed replica receives no messages, sends
none, and does not run its idle logic, but keeps its state, since a
replica that lost its memory is the recovery protocol's job and that
does not exist yet. The per-tick crash and restart probabilities and
their stability periods are drawn from the seed like every other
option. Any replica can crash, including the primary.

The liveness phase now picks a core, a random majority of replicas,
brings it up, and crashes everything else for good, after TigerBeetle's
liveness testing: the protocol promises progress as long as a majority
is up, so the core must converge on its own. Convergence and the final
property checks consider the core only. Tests and runs that are not
about losing the primary can ask for a full core.

Without view changes, a core that excludes the primary cannot make
progress, and that is the point: this is the failing test for view
changes. For example

    SEED=5 cargo run --release -p vsr-simulator -- --lite

picks core [1, 2], crashes the primary for good, and fails with
"no state convergence: pending commit". Seeds whose core keeps the
primary still pass, crashes and all.

Re-send a client request that got no reply, and fault client messages

A client sent its request once. If the network lost it, nothing ever
re-sent it, so the request was gone for good and the simulator had to
keep client messages exempt from faults.

Following the paper (section 4.1), the client keeps its pending request
and on an idle period re-sends it to every replica, since the primary
may have changed without the client knowing. Backups ignore client
requests instead of asserting they are the primary. The client table
added in dd5bbb8 makes the re-sends safe: the primary drops a duplicate
of a request in progress and answers one that already committed from
the table.

The simulator now runs the clients' idle logic on the heartbeat
interval alongside the replicas', and Options::swarm faults client
messages for half the seeds. The --fault-client-messages flag forces
it on. Every seed tried with client loss and replay passes both phases.

Add a cluster test where the request is lost, the client re-sends it
on idle, and after the reply it stops re-sending.

Add the client table so a re-sent request is not executed twice

The primary appended every Request it received to the log, so a request
that reached it twice, because the client re-sent it or the network
replayed it, ran twice. The paper's client table (section 4.1, step 2)
records each client's latest request number and, once executed, the
result. A request numbered at or below that is a re-send: if it is the
latest request and has executed, the primary re-sends the reply from
the table, otherwise it drops the request and the reply follows when
the original commits.

To maintain the table on backups too, which a view change will need,
log entries now carry the client id and request number along with the
op, and so do Prepare messages and the log in NewState. Replies are a
message carrying the client id, request number, and result, since a
client must be able to tell which request a reply answers and discard
duplicates. StateMachine::Output must therefore be Clone. Client::new
takes a client id instead of hardcoding 0, and on_request returns the
request number so the caller can match the reply.

The simulator tracks the outstanding request number per client and
counts a reply as progress only for that request. The property that
checked one reply per commit now checks that every reply is for a
committed request and carries the right result, allowing duplicates,
and at the end that every committed request was replied to. Client
messages are still exempt from network faults; enabling them is next.

Add a cluster test where the same request reaches the primary twice
while it is being prepared, and once more after it committed.

Count PrepareOk acknowledgements per replica, not per message

The primary kept a plain counter of PrepareOk messages per op and
committed when the counter reached the quorum. Two acknowledgements
from the same backup therefore looked like two backups. That happens
routinely: the network can replay a PrepareOk, and since idle periods
re-send uncommitted Prepares, a backup that already has the op
acknowledges it again. With four or more replicas the primary could
reach the quorum with its own entry plus one backup counted twice, and
commit an op that only two replicas held. A view change could then
lose that op even though the client had a reply for it.

The paper's PrepareOk carries the sender's id for this reason. Add
replica_id to the message and keep, for each uncommitted op, the set of
replicas that acknowledged it; commit when the set reaches the quorum.
With three replicas the quorum is two, which one real backup always
satisfies, so the bug never showed at that size.

Add a cluster test with four replicas where only one backup gets the
Prepare and its PrepareOk arrives twice: the primary must not commit
until the re-sent Prepare reaches another backup.

Found by the durability property added in 642b3dc, with:

    SEED=9 cargo run --release -p vsr-simulator

which failed at tick 30 with the op at index 0 committed while 2 of 4
replicas held it. With this fix that seed and every other swarm seed
tried, up to seven replicas, pass both phases.

Add a durability property to the simulator

Every op the primary has committed must be in the log of a majority of
replicas. The primary commits on a quorum of PrepareOk messages and a
backup only acknowledges an op once it is in its log, so this must hold
at the tick the commit happens, and since logs are never truncated each
committed index needs checking once.

This fails today on every cluster of four or more replicas with packet
replay, for example:

    SEED=9 cargo run --release -p vsr-simulator

fails at tick 30 with the op at index 0 committed while only 2 of 4
replicas hold it. The primary counts PrepareOk messages rather than
tracking which replica sent them, so a replayed ack from one backup
counts twice and completes a quorum on its own. With three replicas the
quorum is two, which one real ack always satisfies, so it does not show.

Collapse the library into a single src/lib.rs

Five of the seven source files were under 70 lines, and everything
outside the crate already went through the re-exports, so the split
bought nothing but indirection. The whole library is under 600 lines
and reads better top to bottom: types, state machine trait, config,
messages, client, replica. Split again along real seams once view
changes and recovery make it grow.

The type aliases that used to live in a private module are now public,
which they effectively were already through the public signatures that
used them. No code changes otherwise.
Run rustfmt over the simulator crate

Move the cluster tests out of src/lib.rs into tests/cluster.rs

They only use the public API, and they are integration tests: a few
replicas and a client driven by hand through a tick function. Rust's
convention is a tests/ directory for those. No test changes.

Add --report to scripts/simulate to summarize recorded results

The summary that a run prints at the end is now also available on its
own, per commit and mode, with the commands to reproduce every failure,
so results can be inspected after an interrupted run or between runs.
Link the original Viewstamped Replication paper in the README
Point the VR Revisited paper link at MIT DSpace

Add scripts/simulate to run the simulator with random seeds for a while

A small orchestrator after TigerBeetle's continuous fuzzing setup: one
worker per core runs the simulator with fresh random seeds, alternating
between lite and full configurations, until a time budget expires. Each
run is recorded as one JSON line with the commit, seed, mode, outcome,
duration, and the command to reproduce it. Logs are kept only for runs
that failed or exceeded the per-run timeout, and the failing commands
are listed at the end. Workers take a lock when appending results so
records never interleave.

Retransmit lost protocol messages from idle periods

The paper's description of normal operation explicitly leaves out
"re-sending protocol messages that haven't received responses", and so
did this implementation. A single lost message could therefore stall
the cluster for good:

- A backup that entered state transfer sent one GetState. If it or the
  NewState reply was lost, the backup stayed in Recovery forever,
  dropping every Prepare and Commit it received.
- If the PrepareOk messages for the last op were lost, or its Prepare
  never reached the backups, the primary held the op uncommitted with
  no way to get more acks. The Commit heartbeat only carries the
  commit number, so backups could not tell they were missing anything.

Use idle periods, which already drive the Commit heartbeat, to retry:

- A backup in Recovery re-sends its GetState from on_idle. Replies are
  merged by range, so several arriving for one transfer are harmless.
- The primary re-sends the Prepare for every op above its commit number
  from on_idle, after the Commit heartbeat.
- A backup that receives a Prepare it already has no longer treats it
  as a duplicate to ignore. It still uses the commit number in the
  message and acknowledges again. PrepareOk now carries the backup's
  own op number, meaning it has every op up to that point, which is
  what the paper says PrepareOk means and what prefix commit relies on.
  A re-sent Prepare can carry a commit number beyond the backup's log,
  so committing is bounded by the op number; the re-sent ops that
  follow close the gap.

Add three cluster tests: a lost GetState, lost PrepareOk messages, and
a Prepare that reaches no backup, each recovered by one idle period.

Found by the simulator at commit c149be7 with:

    SEED=7008082073273156606 cargo run --release -p vsr-simulator -- --lite

which stopped with "no state convergence: pending request" after the
full tick budget: replica 2 lost its GetState at tick 7 and replica 1
lost its GetState at tick 142, leaving the primary with five ops it
could never commit. With this change every lossy seed tried so far,
lite and full swarm up to seven replicas, passes both phases.

Use the suffix of a stale NewState instead of asserting on it

A backup in state transfer accepted any NewState as the answer to its
current GetState and asserted that the reply started at its op number.
Nothing ties a reply to the request it answers, so when the network
delayed or replayed a GetState from an earlier transfer, the primary's
reply to that copy arrived during a later transfer, started before the
backup's current op number, and tripped the assertion. The paper leaves
out "filtering of duplicate messages"; this is one of the cases it
covers.

on_new_state now compares the reply's range with the log. In a single
view the overlapping entries are identical, so a reply that starts at or
before the current op number and ends beyond it is still useful: append
only the entries past the log and finish the transfer. A reply that
starts past the log or ends inside it brings nothing usable, so the
backup keeps waiting for another. The commit number in a stale reply
can be lower than the backup's own, so that check becomes a lower
bound.

Add a cluster test where a backup's GetState is replayed, its next
transfer's GetState is lost, and the reply to the replayed copy arrives
during the second transfer covering both the old and the missing
entries.

Found by the simulator at commit 7cf58fa with:

    SEED=8711571497407488070 cargo run --release -p vsr-simulator -- --lite

which panicked at src/replica.rs:275 on tick 57 with op_number_start 8
against op number 13. With this fix the seed no longer fails a safety
property; it stops with "no state convergence: pending request"
because the last PrepareOk messages were lost and nothing retransmits.

Commit the whole log prefix when an op reaches a quorum

When the primary received a quorum of PrepareOk messages for op n, it
executed only log entry n-1 and bumped commit_number by one. That
assumes op n-1 was already committed, which is not guaranteed: the
PrepareOk messages for n-1 can all be lost, or the ones for n can
overtake them. In that case the primary executed op n in op n-1's slot,
replied to the client from the wrong state, and later executed op n-1
out of order when its own acks finally arrived. Backups commit strictly
in log order from the commit number in Prepare and Commit messages, so
their state diverged from the primary's.

The paper (section 4.1, step 5) says that a quorum for op n commits n
and every earlier op, and that the primary executes the earlier ones
first. This is safe because backups only acknowledge an op once they
have every earlier op in their log, so the quorum for n is also a
quorum for everything before it. on_prepare_ok now commits every entry
from commit_number up to n, in order, replying to the client for each,
and then drops the ack counters for the committed ops. A PrepareOk for
an op that is already committed is ignored.

Add a cluster test that drops every PrepareOk for op 1 and checks that
a quorum for op 2 commits both ops in order on the primary and, after
a commit heartbeat, on the backups.

Found by the simulator at commit d270079 with:

    SEED=11056962173458606836 cargo run --release -p vsr-simulator

which failed the state-matches-committed-log property at tick 57 with
the primary having applied op 6 at log index 4. With this fix the seed
runs on to tick 78, where it fails on a separate issue: a stale
NewState reply from an earlier state transfer arrives during a later
one and trips the op_number_start assertion in on_new_state.
Add testing instructions for coding agents

Drop Prepare messages while a backup is in state transfer

A backup that sees a gap in op numbers enters state transfer and asks
the primary for the log from its current op number. Until now it kept
accepting Prepare messages while waiting, so delayed Prepares for the
missing ops were appended and the log moved past the point it had asked
to be repaired from. When NewState finally arrived, the assertion that
op_number_start matches the backup's op number fired.

The paper (section 4.1) says replicas take part in normal-case
processing only when their status is normal, so on_prepare now returns
early otherwise. The NewState reply then applies cleanly, and a later
Prepare that still leaves a gap simply triggers another state transfer.

Add a cluster test that delivers Prepares to one backup in reverse
order, which reproduces the failure deterministically.

Found by the simulator at commit 8b1271c with:

    SEED=11056962173458606836 cargo run --release -p vsr-simulator

which panicked at src/replica.rs:255 on tick 25. That seed still fails
later on a separate bug where the primary commits a single op instead
of the log prefix.

Replace simulation test with a VOPR-style deterministic simulator

Add a simulator/ workspace crate modeled on TigerBeetle's VOPR. The seed
drives the whole configuration: replica count, client count, request
rate, idle periods, heartbeat interval, and network loss, replay, and
delay are all drawn from the seed's PRNG. A run has a safety phase with
faults active until every request is replied to, and a liveness phase
with faults disabled in which the cluster must converge.

Properties checked every tick: commit number monotonic, state machine
matches the committed log prefix, committed prefix agreement across
replicas, no duplicate ops, replies match commits, and convergence at
the end.

The seed can be a git commit hash, and CI runs the simulator with the
commit under test so failures reproduce from the commit alone. Panics in
replica code are caught so the seed is always printed.

Replica gains read-only accessors so properties can inspect it. The old
tests/simulation_test.rs is removed; simulator/simulator_tests.rs checks
the simulator itself for determinism and a few fixed configurations.
Forward state machine apply() result to clients

Use view_number in on_prepare()

We assert that `view_number` is the same as `self.view_number` so let's
just use the former to make the code a bit shorter.
Comment the normal operation flow some more

Drop mutex from Config

Drop the mutex from `Config` to move towards a single-threaded design,
which simplifies the code.

Make NewState handling more robust

Let's verify that the NewState message that we received repairs the log
from the op number that we sent in GetState message. This allows us to
detect cases where we receive duplicate NewState messages and avoid
appending the ops on our log more than once.
Extract message handlers in separate functions

commit.message:
Switch to parking_lot

It's faster & smaller.

Fix commit handling when behind the primary

We obviously cannot just bindly commit because we could be behind the
primary. 🙈 Spotted by the simulator!

Send PrepareOk after state transfer

The simulator found a corner case where we fail to acknowledge a write
and, therefore, not apply the state machine on the primary.

First, the client receives a request, but `Prepare` message never
arrives to one of the replicas:

  Primary <- Request(req=0)
  Backup 1 <- Prepare(op=1)
  Backup 2 <- DROP Prepare(op=1)
  Primary <- PrepareOk(op=1)

As quorum is reached, so primary applies the op to the state machine,
and completes the request.

However, now another request arrives to the client, but this time
`Prepare` message doesn't arrive to the *other* replica. But the replica
that does receive the `Prepare` message is behind in the log, so it
initiates a state transfer:

  Primary <- Request(req=1)
  Backup 1 <- DROP Prepare(op=2)
  Backup 2 <- Prepare(op=2)
  Primary <- GetState(id=2)
  Backup 2 <- NewState(op=2)

However, after the state transfer, we must acknowledge the op; otherwise
primary will just keep waiting forever. Please note that if we did
heartbeats, this issue would be solved once a timer fires, but we should
acknowledge the op immediately anyway.
Add test case for normal operation
Switch to interior mutability in `Client` and `Replica`
